opening.headline: When there are multiple risk paths, you learn how to rank them based on impact and likelihood, providing justification for determining which one to mitigate first.
body: Five risk pathways have been identified: injection in search documents and web pages, tool privilege abuse, external model manipulation, and prompt leakage. However, the team can only address one or two items within a fiscal quarter. When all seem equally important, the more prominent voices tend to take precedence.

In this class, we examine how threats are evaluated along two axes—impact and likelihood—and explore the limitations of such calculations. We also discuss the criteria for selecting four response strategies to risks. Subsequently, we compare OWASP LLM06 excessive privileges with LLM03 supply chain characteristics, and explain why reducing privileges can simultaneously lower the rankings across multiple attack vectors.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Risk paths can be evaluated in terms of impact and likelihood.
It is possible to assess whether path-based priorities are reasonable based on evidence.

screens.title: It is impossible to block everything.
screens.lead: First, review the choice the team encountered. The diagram compares five candidates with the volume that can be handled in one quarter.

visual.alt: A diagram comparing five card candidates for risky paths and two small boxes indicating one quarter of work volume.

paragraphs: After completing the threat modeling, five potential risk paths emerged: injection via search documents, injection via web pages, tool privilege abuse, external model manipulation, and system prompt leakage. All of these are plausible real-world occurrences, and upon hearing their descriptions, they all appear to be significant.

The issue is that personnel and time are limited to just a few items per quarter. Without clear criteria, decisions tend to default to the most recent incident, the strongest claim made by a vocal individual, or the most familiar technology. Such decisions often lack justification and become difficult to explain when questioned later.
The question of this class is this: How do we determine what to block first, and on what basis?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: To assign a rank is also to overlook the rest; the reason for overlooking must be recorded.

screens.outro: First, let us recall what standard we have established so far.

screens.title: When resources are limited, what should be restricted first?
screens.lead: When a question is selected, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. There are no input or submission fields, so first reflect on your own experiences.

items.prompt: When resources are limited, what gets restricted first?
items.answer: The most common response begins with something similar to the just-occurred incident. While this is natural, it does not guarantee that the next thought will take the same form. Comparing pathways with significant influence and high probability, supported by evidence, reduces the tendency to be pulled by recent memory.

items.prompt: Was this judgment based on the extent of the damage, or based on familiarity?
items.answer: The issue with familiar technologies tends to be addressed first because it's easy to resolve. However, ease of resolution does not equate to importance. To establish the extent of potential damage, one must first explain what breaks when that path is compromised.

items.prompt: Can we describe the scope affected when a risk occurs?
items.answer: The scope is determined by the connected tools and data, not by the model. Agents with read-only access and agents capable of deletion and transmission experience completely different impacts even when subjected to the same injection. To say that there is an impact means that one understands the associated permissions.

screens.outro: Now I will summarize the method of assessing risks based on impact and likelihood.

screens.title: Assess by impact×likelihood and select response actions
screens.lead: Select each tab to review the evaluation criteria and corresponding response methods sequentially. On the last tab, you can determine the rankings and verify the four response options for each threat.

tabs.label: Impact
tabs.body: The impact is what and to what extent something breaks when the path is compromised. It's easier to understand by considering how much of confidentiality, integrity, or availability is compromised. When data leaves the system, confidentiality is affected; when records are altered or deleted, integrity is affected; when services stop, availability is affected. OWASP explains that this impact depends on the system with which LLMs interact.

tabs.label: Possibility
tabs.body: The likelihood is determined by whether an attacker can reach a path, and how easy it is to reach. Assess whether the path is publicly accessible, whether special permissions are required, or whether it is known to have vulnerabilities. Paths with high impact and high likelihood should be prioritized. Even if the impact is low, mitigation is required if the likelihood is high; conversely, if the impact is low, even a high likelihood path can be deferred.

tabs.label: The limits of computation
tabs.body: OWASP explains that theoretically the score should be the product of likelihood and impact, yet they note that both factors are difficult to assess and that the cost of fixing the issue is not reflected in this product. Therefore, they do not rely solely on numbers, but instead provide a one-line rationale for each cell, explaining why it was placed there. The rankings are not final and are continuously re-evaluated whenever the system changes.

tabs.label: Four responses
tabs.body: Each threat is addressed with one response. Mitigation involves taking actions to reduce the likelihood; removal involves eliminating the component or functionality that causes the threat. Transfer involves shifting contractual or financial responsibilities to another party, and does not reduce the threat itself, so the responsible party for remaining controls and residual risks must be clearly identified. Acceptance is when mitigation, removal, and transfer are all impractical, and it involves acknowledging the risk; the rationale for acceptance must be documented.

screens.outro: Having verified the criteria, let's now actually display the five paths on the table.

screens.title: List five risk paths on the impact×likelihood matrix.
screens.lead: Each row in the table represents an evaluation of a single path. Assess the validity of the ranking by reading the impact, likelihood, and supporting rationale together.

data.caption: Risk pathway five impact and likelihood assessment and placement rationale
rows: An Indirect Injection in a Search Document
Varying depending on the connected tool
If external parties can write content to the search repository, the entrance is open, and the damage is determined by the subsequent tool permissions.
Whether it's hallucination or injection or any other manipulation, it triggers the result of tool invocation. Its impact grows regardless of the path it encounters.
The model is a binary black box, making it difficult to verify through static analysis and leading to delayed detection. Although the likelihood is low, it is still included in the mitigation items.
If the prompt contains no secrets, exposure causes limited damage. If secrets are present, the impact cell is re-evaluated.
If a vulnerability is known, it is high.
Publicly disclosed vulnerabilities are known to attackers. If they can be fixed with an update, the effort required is small, making them ideal to address first.
data.notes: This table is not a one-time document. Whenever additional tools are added or new data sources are connected, the likelihood and impact cells may change, requiring re-evaluation at those times. By documenting the basis for prioritization, discussions can occur using non-numeric justifications when disputes arise regarding rankings. The reading order should first identify rows with the greatest impact, and then prioritize those with higher likelihood or easier adjustability. In this table, row B becomes a top candidate for initial examination because it amplifies the impact of other rows. Conversely, row D's ranking changes whenever the assumption of transparency is invalidated.

screens.outro: In the table, row B and row C have very different characteristics. Let's compare these two risks side by side.

screens.title: LLM06 Excessive Permissions and LLM03 Supply Chain
screens.lead: Compare how the two risks differ by alternately selecting between them. The causes, the center of response, and the scope of control are all different.

states.label: LLM06 Excessive permissions
states.body: A vulnerability arises when large language models (LLMs) are granted excessive functionality, excessive permissions, and excessive autonomy in their invoked extensions, leading to harmful behaviors such as unexpected or manipulated outputs, regardless of causes like hallucinations or prompt injection. The damage is determined by the tool's permissions. Mitigation strategies include extension minimization, functionality minimization, avoiding open extensions, permission minimization, executing actions within the user context, and requiring human approval for high-impact actions. This presents a significant risk because the areas directly under my control are broad.

states.label: LLM03 Supply Chain
states.body: Risks arising from third-party models, datasets, adapters like LoRA, packages, and licenses. Examples include outdated or poorly maintained models, vulnerable pre-trained models, and models with weak provenance. Models are essentially binary black boxes, making static analysis limited in scope, and published models often lack strong provenance guarantees. Therefore, verification and provenance management, along with component inventory, become central to the process. Because the areas under my direct control are limited, the decision on which components to adopt during the onboarding phase becomes especially critical.

screens.outro: Now let's apply LLM06 to a real-world scenario to see how reducing privileges affects the ranking.

screens.title: Explanation: Why excessive permissions should be blocked first
screens.lead: The instructor demonstrates the process of how permission restrictions can change the ranking using a single example. Press the start button and use the arrow to advance step by step.

steps.title: Context: Document Summary Agent and Extension
steps.body: Document summary agent is using an extended version that not only reads documents but also supports modification and deletion functions. In the previously created table, this path is placed in the cells that have significant impact. Due to its associated high privileges, and because this agent reads external inputs such as search documents.

steps.title: Step 1: The result is the same regardless of the cause.
steps.body: Whether due to injection, hallucination, or simple malfunction, if the model generates a delete call, the tool produces the same result. OWASP describes Excessive Agency as a vulnerability that causes harmful behavior in LLMs, regardless of the underlying cause of malfunction.

steps.title: Step 2: First limit the size of the result.
steps.body: Blocking all possible causes takes a long time and is never complete. On the other hand, the size of the result decreases immediately when permissions are reduced. It is more effective to first limit the size of the result before blocking each individual cause.

steps.title: Step 3: Choose the response
steps.body: If the deletion feature is entirely unused in business operations, then the simplest approach is to remove it entirely from the feature set. If deletion is necessary, mitigate the risk by implementing read-only permissions, executing the operation within the user context, and requiring user approval prior to deletion. Previously, responsibility was shifted without reducing risk, and acceptance requires documentation of justification—thus, this scenario does not apply.

steps.title: Step 4: A cell moves within the table.
steps.body: Reducing privileges lowers the impact. Even if the likelihood of injection remains high, the reduced impact lowers the risk ranking. Other paths, for example, web page injection, are also affected by the same tool, so their impact decreases as well.

steps.title: Conclusion: Permission restrictions reduce multiple paths simultaneously.
steps.body: Permission restrictions reduce the impact of multiple paths with a single action. Therefore, excessive permissions should be the first candidate to be blocked. However, this is a judgment specific to this case, and the table must be re-evaluated when the system changes. If the agent in this case is changed to read-only, this path significantly decreases in impact within the same table.

screens.outro: Having verified the logic of changing rankings through examples, I will now summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaways
screens.lead: Summarize the core of the lesson and consider the impact that would be most immediately affected in your system.

paragraphs: Risk pathways are evaluated along two axes: impact and likelihood, and are mitigated based on high-impact scenarios. Numerical calculations have limitations, so one-line justifications are provided for each pathway. Responses are selected from one of four options: mitigation, elimination, transference, or acceptance, with the note that transference does not reduce the risk itself.

Excessive permissions amplify damage regardless of the root cause, so reducing permissions simultaneously mitigates impacts across multiple pathways. Supply chain risks are limited to a narrow scope and thus rely on verification and source management. Rankings are reassessed whenever the system changes.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: Setting priorities means that deferred items have been created. Deferred items must be recorded with their reasons and must be retrievable for review in the following period. The habit of documenting tables and justifications reduces priority disputes.

glossary.def: This method evaluates risk along two axes: the magnitude of potential loss and the ease with which it might occur. Since both factors are difficult to quantify, the rationale for their assignment is stated together.
There is a risk that unexpected or manipulated outputs could become harmful behaviors due to extensive functionality, permissions, and autonomy.
Risks arising from third-party models, datasets, adapters, and packages. Manipulation or contamination is possible.
A decision to allocate limited resources from a significant source and to document the rationale for deferred items.

misconceptions.myth: Mitigate risks with high potential first.
misconceptions.fact: Possibility alone is insufficient. Paths with significant impact must be addressed even if their likelihood is low, while paths with minor impact can be deferred even if their likelihood is high.

misconceptions.myth: Excessive permissions issues disappear once prompt injection is prevented.
misconceptions.fact: Hallucinations or simple failures also cause the same damage through tool calls. Rather than blocking all causes, it is more effective to reduce tool permissions to limit the scale of the resulting damage.

misconceptions.myth: Priority is set once and remains valid thereafter.
misconceptions.fact: The impact and possibilities change when tools, data sources, or permissions change. The system is re-evaluated each time it changes.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Mitigates impact from a significant source.
Leave one line of justification for each entry in the Impact×Possibility Matrix.
Excessive permissions cause damage regardless of the root cause, so permission restrictions reduce risks across multiple pathways.
Supply chain risks are addressed through verification and source management.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What is the most impactful path in our system, and what is the first action to mitigate it?

checks.q: Document summary: The deletion function of the document agent is completely unused in operations. What is the simplest way to address this risk pathway?
options: The contract delegates responsibility to the vendor by providing an extension with a deletion feature.
Removes the extension with deletion functionality from the configuration to eliminate the cause functionality.
Since the likelihood is low, no action is taken and it is accepted and recorded without intervention.
First strengthen prompt leakage defense to reduce deletion risks.
checks.explain: Unnecessary features should be removed as the simplest response. Previously, responsibility was shifted without reducing the actual risk; acceptance requires documenting rationale, and even if other paths are blocked, the impact of this path remains unchanged.

wrong.0: Risk prior to mitigation does not reduce likelihood or impact.
wrong.2: To accept something, one must leave evidence of the basis for receiving it, and significant pathways must be prepared for even if the likelihood is low.
wrong.3: Prompt leakage is a different pathway and does not mitigate the impact of delete permissions.

checks.intro: In a scenario where the delete function is not in use, choose the simplest possible response. The result will not be recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes, removing unnecessary features by excluding them from the configuration is the simplest approach.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Shifting responsibility or accepting it without documentation leaves the source of risk unchanged.

checks.q: First, reduce excessive permissions to lower the risk ranking, and consider this logic in sequence.
items: Injection, hallucination, or malfunction—whatever the cause, tool invocation produces the same result.
It's often more effective to limit the size of the outcome before blocking all causes.
Read-only permission, user context execution, and deletion approval reduce impact.
The risk ranking decreases even if the impact lowers, despite the increased likelihood of injection.
checks.explain: The impact is independent of the cause and is determined by tool permissions; thus, reducing permissions lowers the impact score and decreases the risk ranking across multiple pathways.
checks.intro: First, reduce the privileges and then examine the logic of rank degradation in sequence. The results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: The logical flow is correct. It begins with an outcome unrelated to its cause and proceeds to reduced impact.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. The observation that results are the same comes first, and the rank change is mentioned at the end.
